title: Computational thinking and complexity
note: Big-O describes how cost grows with input size n, as an upper bound that ignores constant factors and lower-order terms. Big-Ω is a lower bound and Big-Θ is a tight bound. Common classes from fastest to slowest: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ), O(n!).

read.title: Counting steps, not seconds
text: A stopwatch tells you how fast code ran on one machine with one input. Engineers want something more portable: how the work grows as the input grows. Big-O notation answers that by counting steps as a function of the input size n and keeping only the dominant term. An algorithm that takes 3n² + 5n + 7 steps is O(n²), because for large n the n² term swamps everything else and constant factors depend on the hardware anyway.

The common classes form a ladder. Constant time, O(1), is indexing into an array. Logarithmic time, O(log n), comes from halving the problem each step, as binary search does. Linear time, O(n), touches each item once. O(n log n) is the cost of good comparison sorting. Quadratic time, O(n²), usually means nested loops. Exponential and factorial times come from trying every subset or every ordering, and they become hopeless even for modest n.

Big-O is an upper bound. Big-Ω is a lower bound, and Big-Θ means both at once. Analysts also say which case they mean: worst case, average case over likely inputs, or amortized cost averaged over a sequence of operations. A dynamic array occasionally copies everything when it grows, yet appends are still O(1) amortized because those copies are rare.
